name: Salt-water / sodium bicarbonate claims
lead: Salt-water and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) practices are household approaches that people fold into grooming routines: baking soda as a mild abrasive for teeth and skin, saltwater rinses, and baking soda as a sports supplement before hard training.[1] Proponents use them to support a cleaner-looking mouth and skin, and, through exercise capacity, a better physique.

Sodium bicarbonate is a common household compound used as an antacid, a mild abrasive, a deodorant ingredient and a sports supplement.[1] Salt-based face cleansers have also been patented, including a mineral-salt face-washing mask.[2]

chain: Used on teeth, skin or in the mouth
Proponents report cleaner-feeling skin and teeth
angle.text: People use baking soda and salt water as inexpensive cleansers and scrubs for skin and teeth, and baking soda as a pre-training supplement aimed at muscular endurance.

infobox: Sodium bicarbonate, table or sea salt
Mouth rinse, scrub, deodorant, sports supplement

paras: Sodium bicarbonate is used in mouthwashes as a mild abrasive and acid neutraliser, in deodorants, and as an antacid.[1] A dissolved teaspoon in cooled boiled water has been described for cleaning the lash base in blepharitis, and a paste for insect bites.[1] It is also taken as a sports supplement to improve muscular endurance, with studies, mostly in males, suggesting it helps most in brief, intense efforts.[1]

Sodium bicarbonate is classed as causing serious eye irritation, and excess intake can cause alkalosis.[1] The American Cancer Society has warned against using it as a cancer treatment, citing unproven effectiveness and potential harm.[1]
No studies found for salt-water or baking-soda facial routines as such. Related research on sodium bicarbonate as an exercise supplement is described in the general sodium bicarbonate literature.[1]

lore.intro: Community discussions mention salt and bicarbonate mostly in passing, in training logs and diet threads, with salt intake often raised in sports contexts.[3]

claims.claim: Baking soda works as a cheap face or teeth scrub.
claims.believers: Proponents say its fine abrasiveness leaves skin and teeth feeling clean at very low cost.
claims.experts: Sodium bicarbonate is documented as a mild abrasive in oral care and household cleaning; its use as a facial scrub is not described in the reference source.[1]

claims.claim: Baking soda before training improves endurance.
claims.believers: Lifters and athletes use it hoping to delay fatigue in hard sets.
claims.experts: Studies, mostly in males, suggest benefit mainly in brief, intense efforts rather than prolonged ones.[1]

claims.claim: Baking soda treats serious disease such as cancer.
claims.experts: The American Cancer Society has warned against it, citing unproven effectiveness and potential harm.[1]

card.summary: Household baking soda and salt-water routines used as cheap scrubs, rinses and pre-training supplements for skin, teeth and physique.
card.note: Baking soda is an eye irritant and excess intake can cause alkalosis.

quick.overview:
These are low-cost household routines: baking soda as a mild abrasive or supplement and salt water as a rinse or cleanser.

People use them for cleaner-feeling skin and teeth and, with baking soda, to support training endurance.
quick.mechanism: Baking soda is a mild alkaline abrasive that neutralises acid; ingested, it buffers acid during intense exercise.
quick.risks: It irritates eyes, and large intakes can cause alkalosis. Claims that it treats cancer have drawn a warning from the American Cancer Society.
